title: The One With All The Candy

jokes.text: No, no. One daddy, two mommies.
jokes.setup: Ben thanks 'Daddy' as Ross helps with his bike helmet, implying a standard parent-child moment.
jokes.punchline: Ross corrects Ben with the exact count of his unconventional family structure — one dad, two moms — delivered matter-of-factly.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly economical joke that only works for Ross specifically — his complicated family situation (divorced from Carol, who is now with Susan) is core character lore. Delivered as a mild correction rather than complaint, which is the ideal tone. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Thanks, Daddy, for helping me with my helmet.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, actually, I'm your father. Daddy is what you call me, but I'm your father.

jokes.text: It was my sixth birthday. My dad took me to the park... and I got on it and... it bent.
jokes.setup: Characters are sharing nostalgic memories of their first bikes in a warm, celebratory moment.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's bike bent under him — a bleak, self-deprecating detail delivered with resigned flatness.
jokes.explanation: Classic Chandler self-deprecation. The timing of the pause before 'it bent' is key — the audience expects something sweet. The bluntness of 'it bent' is the entire joke. Very on-brand for Chandler's brand of sad-funny delivery.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I remember my first bike... it was beautiful. I rode it everywhere.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: For about thirty seconds, until it completely collapsed under me.

jokes.text: So I would sit on it and my stepdad would drag me around the backyard.
jokes.setup: Phoebe describes never having a bike of her own but getting the box it came in with a picture of a bike on the front.
jokes.punchline: Rather than this being entirely sad, Phoebe reveals she made it work — sitting on the box while her stepdad dragged her. It's both bleak and oddly triumphant.
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional Phoebe writing. The escalation from 'no bike' to 'got the box' to 'sat on the box picture and was dragged around' hits three distinct comedic beats in rapid succession. It's deeply character-specific — only Phoebe's deprived childhood makes this joke land — and the detail is specific enough to feel real rather than manufactured. Earns its 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: So I never got to ride it. But I did ride an empty box down the stairs.

jokes.text: That is so unfair. / Not really, I got to drag him around too.
jokes.setup: Ross says it's unfair that Phoebe had to make do with just the box, implying he sympathizes with her being dragged.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe clarifies it was mutual — she dragged her stepdad too — reframing the whole image as a weird shared activity rather than pure deprivation.
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's rejoinder flips the sympathy framing neatly. The image of two people taking turns dragging each other on a cardboard box is absurd and sad simultaneously, which is Phoebe's comedic sweet spot.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: That's so sad. I'm sorry you had to go through that.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, it wasn't sad. We were just messing with you.

jokes.text: ...and the red-haired guy who does not like to be called Rusty.
jokes.setup: Ross lists his neighbors by their physical descriptors rather than names, showing how disconnected they are.
jokes.punchline: The final neighbor is identified by a name he specifically does NOT want — implying Ross learned this detail through an uncomfortable interaction.
jokes.explanation: Smart comedic logic — the fact that 'does not like to be called Rusty' IS the most specific thing Ross knows implies a prior awkward encounter. The joke rewards inference. Good economy; the list structure builds well.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I don't really know our neighbors that well. There's that redhead who lives across the hall, and I know she prefers to be called by her first name, not her last name.

jokes.text: Wouldn't it be easier if we just moved?
jokes.setup: Monica explains she's making candy to meet the neighbors and get to know them.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's immediate alternative — just move — reveals his antisocial nature and the absurdity of Monica's project through contrast.
jokes.explanation: Functional Chandler-style deflection. The logic is absurdly disproportionate (moving vs. making candy) which is funny, but it's a fairly standard 'anti-effort' joke type for the character.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I really think we should get to know the neighbors better.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Or, we could just set off a nuclear device in the building. That way, we'd never have to see them again.

jokes.text: Where you can make out with your assistant.
jokes.setup: Rachel brags about her wonderful job in an upbeat monologue.
jokes.punchline: Chandler immediately punctures her enthusiasm by naming the specific, problematic perk — making out with Tag.
jokes.explanation: Solid interruption comedy. The timing of cutting off Rachel's self-congratulation works well, but the joke itself is fairly basic — it's just naming the elephant in the room bluntly.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Okay, so here's the plan. I'm going to ask her out, we'll go on a few dates, and then... we'll see where it goes from there.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Wow. A master plan. That's... that's actually just dating.

jokes.text: We... We are not... going to let it... be a problem. / Wow. It took you all night to come up with that plan?
jokes.setup: Rachel boasts that she and Tag came up with a plan overnight to ensure their dating won't be a workplace problem.
jokes.punchline: The 'plan' is revealed to be nothing — just a decision not to let it be a problem — which Chandler immediately skewers.
jokes.explanation: The delivery of the 'plan' — stretched across multiple hesitant beats — is what elevates this. Rachel's trailing, embarrassed explanation followed by Chandler's withering response is well-structured. The joke depends on Jennifer Aniston's performance timing.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I've slept with guys on first dates. I'm not that girl anymore.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Wait, no. I mean I haven't slept with guys on first dates.

jokes.text: Oh, well, you know, we did other stuff too. [Chandler and Joey chuckle] Did you two?
jokes.setup: Rachel admits the 'plan' was nothing, then adds they 'did other stuff too' — meaning they were intimate.
jokes.punchline: Chandler and Joey immediately giggle at the implication; Monica's dry 'Did you two?' calls it out directly.
jokes.explanation: Standard innuendo catch. Chandler and Joey's juvenile giggling is characterful, and Monica's flat 'Did you two?' is a good reaction beat, but the joke itself is fairly telegraphed.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Tag, I need to talk to you about something. I've been thinking... maybe we should work together more closely.

dialogue.speaker: Tag
dialogue.line: Really? What did you have in mind?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, I need you to help me with something very important. It's going to require us to be in very close proximity.

dialogue.speaker: Tag
dialogue.line: Oh wow, okay...

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I need you to help me clear these papers off my desk dramatically.

jokes.text: Oh, Monica, you know I don't sleep with guys on the first date. / Matt Wire, Mark Lynn, Ben Wise... / Anymore.
jokes.setup: Rachel claims moral high ground — she doesn't sleep with guys on first dates.
jokes.punchline: Monica immediately recites three full names as counterexamples; Rachel concedes with a single word: 'Anymore.'
jokes.explanation: Exceptional comedic economy. The joke structure is near-perfect: Rachel's self-righteous claim, Monica's devastating three-name rebuttal (the specificity of full names is key — it implies Monica memorized them), and Rachel's one-word concession. 'Anymore' does enormous work in a single syllable. This is the kind of well-engineered joke that earns its score.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Joey! Did you eat all the candy?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, I ate some of it.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Some? The basket is completely empty!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I barely got any! Most of it was already gone when I got there.

jokes.text: Rachel dismisses the mail guy elaborately to make their relationship look professional, then Tag immediately follows her into her office
jokes.setup: Rachel performs an exaggerated, cold professional dismissal of Tag in front of the mail guy to prove their relationship is secret.
jokes.punchline: Tag immediately follows her back into the office, completely undermining the charade.
jokes.explanation: Physical/visual situational comedy — the irony of their elaborate secrecy being instantly undone is functional. Works better as a visual than it reads in transcript form.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Monica, can you make more of that candy? I ate it all.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Joey, that was for the party tonight!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I know, I know. And uh, I may have also... sampled the lasagna.

jokes.text: Did you see that? That mail guy had no idea there was something going on between us.
jokes.setup: Rachel performed an over-the-top professional dismissal of Tag and is now proud of herself.
jokes.punchline: Her self-congratulation is the joke — the audience has just seen Tag immediately follow her into the office, so her confidence is absurd.
jokes.explanation: Rachel's obliviousness to how obvious they are is a running theme of this subplot. Functional irony, though it relies heavily on the visual context of Tag having just followed her in.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh, so because someone stole a newspaper, suddenly we're living in a crime wave? Monica, last week you made those amazing brownies and gave them to the whole building. By your logic, that's also a crime wave—a delicious crime wave.

jokes.text: But you know, there is one thing that I have yet to evaluate... [sweeps desk clean]
jokes.setup: Rachel tells Tag she needs to hand in his performance evaluation and mentions there's something she hasn't evaluated yet — the audience expects a professional context.
jokes.punchline: She sweeps her desk completely clear and pulls him toward her — the 'evaluation' is entirely physical/romantic.
jokes.explanation: The desk-sweep is a classic romantic/comedic gesture that gets a reliable laugh through the visual absurdity. Somewhat clichéd as a rom-com trope, but executed crisply.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Are you crying?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: No, I'm not crying. There's just something in my eye.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Your tear?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Could be.

jokes.text: Are you serious? / No, I've just always wanted to do that.
jokes.setup: Tag reacts with shock to Rachel sweeping everything off her desk.
jokes.punchline: Rachel admits it had nothing to do with evaluation — she just always wanted to perform that dramatic desk-sweep move.
jokes.explanation: This reframe is clever — it acknowledges that the desk-sweep is itself a movie trope Rachel has always wanted to perform, adding a layer of meta self-awareness to what could have been a straight romantic moment. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What time is it?

dialogue.speaker: Gary
dialogue.line: It's candy o'clock.

jokes.text: Can you help me clean this up?
jokes.setup: Rachel has just had a dramatic, romantic desk-sweep moment with Tag.
jokes.punchline: She immediately follows the romance with a completely practical request to help tidy up the mess she made.
jokes.explanation: The speed of the deflation is what makes this work. Going from romantic movie trope to 'can you help me clean this up' in one beat is pitch-perfect comic timing. Pure economy — four words do all the heavy lifting.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Some of us have to work early tomorrow.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I don't actually have to work.

jokes.text: Joey, did you eat all the neighbor candy? / Uh, well, yeah, that was the plan. But by the time I got to it there was only a couple pieces left.
jokes.setup: Monica discovers the candy basket is empty and suspects Joey.
jokes.punchline: Joey admits eating it was indeed 'the plan' but then reveals the neighbors beat him to most of it — he only got the dregs.
jokes.explanation: Classic Joey food joke with a twist — he fully admits his intent to eat the candy was 'the plan,' and then his genuine grievance that the neighbors beat him to it flips the guilt. Very character-specific; Joey's total lack of remorse about planning to steal the candy is perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I may have written some personal stuff.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Like, really personal stuff.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I wrote that he had the best smile in the office and that I loved the way his eyes crinkle when he laughs.

jokes.text: Hey, Mon. Make some more lasagna too. Something might have happened to a huge chunk of it.
jokes.setup: Monica is rushing to make more candy after the neighbors ate it all.
jokes.punchline: Joey casually also requests more lasagna, using the euphemism 'something might have happened to it' to describe his having eaten it.
jokes.explanation: The passive construction 'something might have happened to a huge chunk of it' is comic gold — Joey is simultaneously confessing and distancing himself from responsibility. Highly character-integrated and wonderfully economical phrasing.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: He said I was 'exceeding expectations' and then asked if I wanted to 'discuss my performance review.'

jokes.text: Ross, the neighbors ate all my candy. / Mine stole my newspaper. / It's like a crime wave.
jokes.setup: Monica complains that the neighbors ate all her candy (a minor frustration).
jokes.punchline: Ross immediately one-ups her with his own 'crime' — a stolen newspaper — and then together they frame both trivial inconveniences as a 'crime wave.'
jokes.explanation: 'Crime wave' is a good button — the disproportionate label for two utterly minor annoyances. The escalation from Monica's complaint to Ross's parallel whine to the shared grandiose conclusion is neatly structured.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: And then he wrote, 'She really knows how to handle a stiff position.'

jokes.text: Ross gives Phoebe a bike. Phoebe says 'I love you. Not that way. But the bike got you a lot closer.'
jokes.setup: Ross gives Phoebe her first bike in a heartfelt moment. Phoebe says 'I love you.'
jokes.punchline: She immediately qualifies 'not that way' — but then adds the bike moved him significantly up her romantic ranking anyway.
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection followed by a secondary twist. The first pivot ('not that way') is expected; the second reveal ('but the bike got you a lot closer') is the actual joke. Good Phoebe characterization — she's completely candid about the sliding scale of her affections.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Why are you getting emotional about Titanic?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm not getting emotional! And it's a very sad movie. Jack dies at the end.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Everyone knows Jack dies.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, I didn't! And it's tragic! A man dies for love!

jokes.text: Oh, and Chandler's about to cry. / Am not.
jokes.setup: Ross gives Phoebe the bike in a genuinely sweet moment. Phoebe runs off excited.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe casually announces Chandler is about to cry; Chandler's immediate denial is itself a tell.
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's psychic-like read on Chandler's emotional state and his defensive 'Am not' is a lovely two-beat joke. Chandler's emotional unavailability is core to his character, and the visual of him visibly moved while denying it would be excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Okay, here, watch this!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: There! I rode it!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Phoebe, you just walked with the bike.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I know what I did.

jokes.text: It's candy time.
jokes.setup: Monica answers the door at 4 a.m. to a neighbor demanding candy.
jokes.punchline: Gary's explanation for why he knocked at 4 a.m. is simply: 'It's candy time.' No other justification.
jokes.explanation: 'It's candy time' is a brilliantly absurd non-answer. The confidence of the delivery — as if 4 a.m. candy visits are completely reasonable — is what makes it so funny. Near-perfect economy (three words, complete idea).

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Do you think they took that the wrong way?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: No, no, I'm sure when they heard you say you spent the last four hours filing your nails, they thought you meant you were at a hardware store.

jokes.text: He does not know that I am not 'some of us.'
jokes.setup: Monica scolds the neighbor about how 'some of us have to get up early and go to work,' trying to maintain the domestic fiction.
jokes.punchline: Monica's internal/talking-head-style confession that she is, in fact, NOT one of the people who has to go to work — she's between jobs — deflates her own self-righteous speech.
jokes.explanation: Monica's self-awareness about her unemployed status undermining her moral high ground is a great internal joke. The way she's just said something with authority and then immediately privately contradicts it is good ironic construction.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, I studied anatomy. I was in this art class, right, and there was this naked model, and I just became obsessed with drawing the human form. Especially the female form.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: So I practiced. A lot. In my apartment. With magazines as reference material.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I got really good at it. Too good, if you ask me.

jokes.text: Mm. Seems like I would have remembered you. / Mm. Night, Gar.
jokes.setup: Gary discovers Monica is his neighbor and implies she's attractive enough that he should have noticed her.
jokes.punchline: Monica immediately adopts an affectionate nickname ('Gar') for someone she met 90 seconds ago — playing along with the flirtation.
jokes.explanation: The instant-nickname ('Gar') after two minutes of acquaintance is a small, charming joke about Monica's warmth/forwardness. Not a major laugh, but a nice character beat.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh my God, I know exactly who you're talking about. That's the woman from 4G.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: How do you know that?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, let's just say her bedroom skills are... very vocal.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh! Yeah, yeah, yeah! I know who you mean!

jokes.text: Okay, please, you're kidding, right? I wrote that one as a joke for you. / A joke they would appreciate? / I'm thinking no.
jokes.setup: Rachel learns the joke evaluation she wrote for Tag was sent to HR as official documentation.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's flat 'A joke they would appreciate? I'm thinking no' perfectly captures the horror of the situation with minimal words.
jokes.explanation: Chandler's 'I'm thinking no' construction is a reliable, well-executed Friends-ism. The two-step — asking the question then answering it — is a good structural choice.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I can't believe my 'no candy after hours' sign didn't work!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Have you tried the other obvious solution?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Eating all the candy before hours.

jokes.text: I said that you were a good kisser... and that I liked your teeny, tiny tushy.
jokes.setup: Rachel has to confess what she actually wrote in Tag's official HR performance evaluation.
jokes.punchline: The evaluation contained 'good kisser' and 'teeny, tiny tushy' — wildly inappropriate workplace documentation.
jokes.explanation: The specific phrase 'teeny, tiny tushy' is memorable and funny — the alliteration and the childish word 'tushy' in an official HR document creates great incongruity. The specificity elevates it above a generic 'inappropriate workplace comment' joke.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I cook so people will like me.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, at least you're honest about it. I tell jokes for the same reason.

jokes.text: No, not my tushy.
jokes.setup: Rachel has just told Tag that his official HR evaluation mentions his 'teeny, tiny tushy.'
jokes.punchline: Tag's distressed response focuses specifically on the tushy detail rather than the larger HR crisis.
jokes.explanation: Good reaction beat. His horror is specifically about the tushy mention, not the relationship exposure, which is a funny priority inversion.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: This bike seat is killing me. My butt is so sore.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You know what I need? A seat made of clouds. Or maybe just a regular chair bolted to the bike frame.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Or I could ride standing up the whole time. Or get one of those bikes where you lie down. Actually, I should just get a horse instead.

jokes.text: When asked if you take initiative, I wrote: 'Yes, he was able to unhook my bra with minimal supervision.'
jokes.setup: Rachel continues recounting the increasingly inappropriate contents of the official evaluation.
jokes.punchline: The formal HR language ('take initiative,' 'minimal supervision') applied to bra-unhooking is a perfect incongruity joke.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. The register clash is perfect — HR boilerplate ('take initiative,' 'minimal supervision') mapped precisely onto a sexual encounter is brilliantly constructed. 'Minimal supervision' in particular is inspired. High originality, great structure, very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Okay, so if you're riding your bike and you suddenly lose the brakes, what do you do?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I'd throw my glitter in the air and make a wish!

jokes.text: And under problems with performance, I wrote: 'Dear God, I hope not.'
jokes.setup: Rachel continues reading her disastrous HR evaluation entries.
jokes.punchline: The 'problems with performance' section — standard HR language — is answered with 'Dear God, I hope not,' an intensely personal and sexual response.
jokes.explanation: The escalation of the evaluation entries is well-managed, and 'Dear God, I hope not' perfectly captures Rachel's personality while also being an excellent innuendo. The formality of the HR framing makes the personal response funnier each time.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You said you wouldn't let go.

jokes.text: And then, uh... And then I drew a little smiley face. / And then a small pornographic sketch.
jokes.setup: Rachel has described three increasingly inappropriate evaluation entries. The smiley face seems like the button.
jokes.punchline: The 'small pornographic sketch' revelation tops the smiley face, taking the escalation one unexpected step further.
jokes.explanation: The two-part delivery — pause on 'smiley face' (which feels like the button), then the additional revelation of the pornographic sketch — is excellent escalation craft. The word 'small' modifying the pornographic sketch adds an absurd touch of modesty.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I'm not obsessive! I'm just... thorough. There's a difference.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Mon, you've made 47 batches of fudge. It's Tuesday.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Exactly! And I need at least 60 batches for the wedding.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Monica, honey, the wedding isn't for six months.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I KNOW! That's why I'm behind schedule!

jokes.text: Hey, you cry every time somebody talks about Titanic. / Those two had only each other.
jokes.setup: Ross points out that Monica 'almost' cried at Phoebe's bike story, teasing Chandler who also got emotional.
jokes.punchline: Chandler accuses Ross of crying at Titanic; Ross's sincere, heartfelt defense ('Those two had only each other') is itself the joke.
jokes.explanation: Ross's earnest defense of his Titanic tears is perfectly in character — his sincerity is the entire joke. 'Those two had only each other' delivered with complete conviction is a great character moment. The joke works because Ross doesn't see the irony.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Come on, Phoebe, just try riding the bike again.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: No way. I can't ride a bike, Ross. I never learned how.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You can do this. I'll help you.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Fine. But if I fall, I'm suing you. Oh wait, my bike got stolen.

jokes.text: Pheebs, you, uh... You do know how to ride a bike, don't you?
jokes.setup: Both Ross and Monica have separately seen Phoebe 'walking' her bike rather than riding it, and the penny drops.
jokes.punchline: Ross's tentative question confirms the audience's dawning suspicion — Phoebe has never actually ridden the bike.
jokes.explanation: Good setup for the Phoebe-can't-ride subplot. The gradual reveal (two sightings of her walking the bike, then the direct question) is well-structured across multiple beats.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: The bike wants to be ridden!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Look at it! It's dying from neglect!

jokes.text: Of course. [All laugh] Can we see you ride it? / Okay. [Falls off bike immediately]
jokes.setup: Phoebe confidently declares she knows how to ride a bike.
jokes.punchline: She immediately falls off, contradicting her confident claim.
jokes.explanation: Classic physical comedy beat. The confidence-then-immediate-failure structure is reliable, and the lack of fanfare before the fall makes it work better. High visual impact.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I know you're just saying that because you feel guilty, but yeah, okay, I'll take the bike.

jokes.text: This is why I told you never get involved with your assistant. And there's no such thing as keeping secrets when it comes to having affairs. / Did you hear that, Chandler? No such thing. / What happened? I'm just eating candy.
jokes.setup: Joey has been eating candy in the background while Ross and Chandler discuss Rachel's workplace relationship disaster.
jokes.punchline: Ross delivers a pointed lesson to Chandler (about their own secrets); Chandler pointedly asks 'Did you hear that?' — and Joey, completely oblivious, only registers the candy-eating accusation.
jokes.explanation: Joey's obliviousness ('What happened? I'm just eating candy') as a counterpoint to Ross and Chandler's loaded exchange is excellent. His complete disconnection from the subtext happening around him is perfectly in character and very funny.

dialogue.speaker: Tag
dialogue.line: I wrote that evaluation about myself. I was just... I was trying to be funny.

dialogue.speaker: Mr. Zelner
dialogue.line: You wrote about your own... posterior?

dialogue.speaker: Tag
dialogue.line: Yeah, I thought it would be a good icebreaker, you know? Get people to loosen up a little bit.

jokes.text: Because 'tushy' can mean both ass... and good worker.
jokes.setup: Rachel is hoping HR didn't take the evaluation the way she meant it.
jokes.punchline: Chandler sarcastically suggests 'tushy' has a professional meaning — 'good worker' — which is obviously absurd.
jokes.explanation: Chandler's fake-helpful reframing is good sarcasm. The invented second meaning of 'tushy' as 'good worker' is delivered with enough straight-faced confidence to land.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, Tag, did you get fired?

dialogue.speaker: Tag
dialogue.line: No, no, no. Remember when I said that thing about your butt? That's not something a guy says right before he loses his job.

jokes.text: I tell you, this little talent came in handy before I could afford porn.
jokes.setup: Joey has apparently drawn a pornographic sketch that matches what Rachel put in the evaluation, suggesting he draws these regularly.
jokes.punchline: Joey admits his sketching talent served as a pre-pornography substitute — delivered with complete matter-of-factness.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout lines. The delivery — total Joey sincerity, sharing a practical life tip — is perfect. It's deeply character-specific (only Joey would say this, and only Joey could make it charming rather than disturbing). The word 'handy' inadvertently does additional work. Near-perfect economy.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Do they know her name?

dialogue.speaker: Neighbor
dialogue.line: We only know her as Candy Lady.

dialogue.speaker: Neighbor
dialogue.line: We just want candy.

jokes.text: Hi, I'm sorry. I know it's after hours, but I really need candy.
jokes.setup: Monica has just been dealing with Gary at 4 a.m. for candy; now another neighbor arrives during what are presumably business hours.
jokes.punchline: The apologetic, desperate framing of needing candy 'after hours' — as if Monica is running a pharmacy — escalates the candy-mania running gag.
jokes.explanation: The 'after hours' framing makes the candy obsession feel like a drug operation, which is a good comedic angle. Functional escalation of the candy subplot.

jokes.text: Well, some people have been saying it's 'little drops of heaven,' but whatever.
jokes.setup: The neighbor says Monica's candy is 'indescribable.' Monica corrects her with the specific superlative she prefers.
jokes.punchline: Monica immediately supplies the preferred phrase ('little drops of heaven') while affecting casual modesty with 'but whatever.'
jokes.explanation: Monica's combination of pride and false modesty is very true to character. The fact that she's carefully tracking what compliments people use about her candy is a sharp character detail. Good callback to the Gary scene.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh wow, that was beautiful Ross. So basically you're saying if we face our fears, we can do anything?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Exactly! That's the whole point.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Because that is so not true. I faced my fear of wearing a dead animal on my head and now I'm just cold and everyone thinks I'm insane.

jokes.text: Maybe. Isn't she the woman who lives below you and has sex really loud?
jokes.setup: Chandler and Monica are asked if they know the desperate candy-seeking neighbor.
jokes.punchline: Chandler identifies her by her most notable characteristic — extremely loud sex — in front of her.
jokes.explanation: Good embarrassment-comedy timing — the neighbor is clearly present for the identification. The logic mirrors the earlier 'neighbors by descriptor' joke but applied now to a more awkward descriptor.

jokes.text: All right, I'll do it just this once. But you can't tell anybody. / Yes, yes, please, just give it to me. / BOTH: Yeah, that's her.
jokes.setup: Monica and the neighbor's exchange about candy sounds exactly like a drug deal.
jokes.punchline: Chandler and Monica both confirm the neighbor's identity ('Yeah, that's her') with the sexual characteristic, confirmed by her own desperate candy-seeking behavior.
jokes.explanation: The drug-deal dialogue ('I'll do it just this once, but you can't tell anybody' / 'Please, just give it to me') combined with the double confirmation of the neighbor's identity is a satisfying multi-layered joke. The candy-as-drugs implication builds well.

jokes.text: I can't believe that sign didn't work. / You know what would work? Stop making candy.
jokes.setup: Monica is frustrated that putting up a sign didn't stop neighbors from demanding candy.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's obvious solution — just stop making it — cuts through Monica's self-delusion.
jokes.explanation: Chandler's practical counterpoint to Monica's obsessive candy-making is good character contrast. Not original but cleanly executed.

jokes.text: Is that why you became a chef, so that people would like you? / Heh. You want to talk about getting people to like you, huh, funny man?
jokes.setup: Chandler psychoanalyzes Monica's candy-making as a need for approval.
jokes.punchline: Monica turns it back on Chandler — implying his entire career as a 'funny man' (or general use of humor) is also about getting people to like him.
jokes.explanation: Monica's riposte is sharp and character-true for both of them. Chandler's use of humor as social armor is a well-established character trait, and Monica weaponizing that insight in one line is good writing.

jokes.text: Wait, this seat is really uncomfortable. Maybe before we start we should just get another one. Perhaps like an airplane seat, or a beanbag chair.
jokes.setup: Ross is about to teach Phoebe to ride her bike.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe delays with an absurd list of alternative seats — escalating from 'airplane seat' to 'beanbag chair' — which are obviously impractical for a bicycle.
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's stalling is in character, and the escalation of seat suggestions (airplane seat, beanbag chair) is appropriately absurd. The specificity of 'beanbag chair' as the final escalation is a good comic choice.

jokes.text: Well, what if a man comes along and puts a gun to your head and says: 'You ride this bike or I'll... I'll shoot you.' / Okay. I would ring the bell to distract him, and then I would knock the gun out of his hand with a Chinese throwing star.
jokes.setup: Ross tries to motivate Phoebe by inventing an emergency scenario where she'd need to ride a bike.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe doesn't engage with the premise — she has an immediate and extremely specific alternative plan involving a bell and a throwing star, rendering the bike irrelevant.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best joke. Ross's hypothetical is already absurd ('a man with a gun demanding you ride a bike'), but Phoebe's response is what makes it extraordinary. She doesn't reject the premise — she engages with it completely seriously and has a BETTER plan. 'Ring the bell to distract him' is inspired, and the Chinese throwing star escalation is perfect Phoebe logic. The joke works on multiple levels: Ross's desperation, Phoebe's matter-of-fact supernatural competence, and the fact that her solution is objectively better than 'just ride the bike.' Exceptional character integration — no other character on TV could deliver this joke.

jokes.text: Okay. I would ring the bell to distract him, and then I would knock the gun out of his hand with a Chinese throwing star.
jokes.setup: Ross presents a scenario where a gunman demands Phoebe ride a bike
jokes.punchline: Phoebe has a fully worked-out alternative plan that doesn't involve the bike — ringing the bell as a distraction, then deploying a Chinese throwing star — delivered as if this is obvious
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The structure is perfect: Ross sets up an absurd scenario expecting to prove Phoebe needs to ride, but she has a detailed counter-plan that makes no assumptions about bike-riding. The specific detail of using the bell as a distraction (the bell being part of the bike) is inspired — she's weaponizing the bike's accessories rather than riding it. The throwing star is the perfect absurdist escalation. Entirely Phoebe — no other character would have this response.

jokes.text: That's it, you're doing great. Yes, take control. / Yes, yes, yes. / Whee! Hey! / Oh, oh! Oh, no. [Ross has let go of the bike]
jokes.setup: Ross promises not to let go of the bike while teaching Phoebe to ride.
jokes.punchline: He lets go — the classic parental bike-teaching betrayal — and Phoebe crashes.
jokes.explanation: The 'parent lets go of bike' gag is one of the most universal and well-worn physical comedy beats in existence. Executed competently here but brings very little original craft — the audience knows exactly what's coming the moment Ross swears he won't let go.

jokes.text: You swore. / I just thought you were doing so well. / I am shocked. Shocked.
jokes.setup: Ross has let go of the bike despite swearing he wouldn't, and Phoebe has crashed.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's repeated 'I am shocked. Shocked.' — with its theatrical emphasis — is funnier than simple anger would be.
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's slightly over-performed outrage ('Shocked. Shocked.') is a good character beat. The repetition and emphasis are funnier than a natural reaction would be.

jokes.text: It's a legitimate learning technique. / Wow.
jokes.setup: Ross has just let go of the bike, causing Phoebe to crash.
jokes.punchline: Ross defends the betrayal as 'a legitimate learning technique'; Chandler's one-word 'Wow' is a perfect deadpan verdict.
jokes.explanation: Ross's academic justification for the bike betrayal ('legitimate learning technique') followed by Chandler's minimal but devastating 'Wow' is a good two-beat. Classic straight-man-and-fool dynamic.

jokes.text: By the way, the week before your wedding, you may not see a lot of me.
jokes.setup: Joey is 'helping' Monica in the kitchen (ostensibly he's just eating).
jokes.punchline: Joey pre-emptively warns Monica that he'll be unavailable the week before her wedding — implying he's going to be doing something selfish and not explaining what.
jokes.explanation: Classic Joey self-absorption joke. The warning is delivered in a helpful tone, as though he's doing Monica a favor by giving notice, completely oblivious to how it sounds. The lack of any explanation for his unavailability makes it funnier.

jokes.text: Oh, hello, liar.
jokes.setup: Ross comes to apologize to Phoebe after letting go of the bike.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe greets him simply as 'liar' — precise, unadorned, devastating.
jokes.explanation: Two words, complete character moment. Phoebe addresses Ross not by name but by his crime — delivered with Phoebe's particular brand of guileless directness. The 'Oh, hello' prefix makes it funnier by implying cheerful greeting before the label. Near-perfect economy.

jokes.text: Well, the bike got stolen and the police have no suspects.
jokes.setup: Ross asks Phoebe if they can try the bike lesson again.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's excuse — the bike was stolen and police have no suspects — is delivered as a solemn report, implying she is both lying and enjoying her lie.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional Phoebe joke. The official-report phrasing ('the police have no suspects') applied to what is obviously her own bike sitting right there is very funny. The deadpan delivery of a transparent lie, combined with the procedural language, is pitch-perfect character comedy. Earns its 8+.

jokes.text: [Bell rings from the 'stolen' bike, which is visibly right there]
jokes.setup: Phoebe has just claimed the bike was stolen.
jokes.punchline: The bike's bell rings — the bike is obviously still there, immediately exposing the lie.
jokes.explanation: Perfect visual comedy. The bike's bell ringing as a silent confession is a brilliantly simple payoff. No dialogue needed — the bell does all the work. The timing (ringing immediately after the claim) is impeccable. This is what great physical comedy writing looks like — maximum impact, zero words.

jokes.text: It'd be like you having this guitar and never playing it. Okay, this guitar wants to be played. And this bike wants to be ridden. And if you don't ride it... you're killing its spirit.
jokes.setup: Ross is trying to guilt Phoebe into trying again by using an extended metaphor.
jokes.punchline: He escalates from a reasonable guitar analogy to 'you're killing its spirit' — the bike now has a spirit that can be murdered by neglect.
jokes.explanation: The escalation from sensible argument to 'you're killing its spirit' is nicely paced. Ross delivering this with paleontologist-level seriousness about an inanimate bicycle is good character comedy.

jokes.text: All right. If you care enough to make up that load of crap, okay.
jokes.setup: Ross delivers an earnest guilt-trip about the bike's dying spirit.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe calls it out directly as 'a load of crap' — but agrees precisely BECAUSE he cared enough to make it up.
jokes.explanation: Smart comedic logic — Phoebe's criterion for agreeing is not whether the argument is true, but whether Ross's effort in fabricating it shows he cares. It's simultaneously a sharp commentary on the manipulation and a sweet character beat. Very Phoebe.

jokes.text: Please don't die.
jokes.setup: Phoebe has agreed to try riding the bike again after Ross's speech about the bike's dying spirit.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe speaks to the bike directly, asking it not to die — she has fully absorbed Ross's framing of the bike as a living being.
jokes.explanation: Three words. Perfect. Phoebe's sincere address to the bike ('Please don't die') is the ideal payoff to Ross's manipulative speech about the bike's spirit. It shows Phoebe has taken his absurd premise completely literally and is now genuinely concerned for the bike's wellbeing. Pure Phoebe, maximally economical, deeply character-integrated. One of the best lines of the episode.

jokes.text: Or, uh, to use his full name, Tag 'Sweet Cheeks' Jones?
jokes.setup: Mr. Zelner announces he read the performance evaluation of Tag.
jokes.punchline: He reveals that the evaluation has introduced a nickname — 'Sweet Cheeks' — which he delivers with formality as if it's official documentation.
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback joke. The deadpan formality — 'to use his full name' as if 'Sweet Cheeks' is an official designation — combined with the bureaucratic register is very funny. Mr. Zelner's straight-faced delivery of the absurd nickname gives it extra power.

jokes.text: You wrote that you have a cute tushy? / Yes. I have a weird sense of humor. And I'm kind of strangely proud of my butt.
jokes.setup: Tag has taken responsibility for the evaluation, claiming he wrote it as a joke about himself.
jokes.punchline: Tag's explanation — 'I'm kind of strangely proud of my butt' — is simultaneously a cover story and apparently genuine, delivered with just enough earnestness.
jokes.explanation: Tag's aside about being 'strangely proud' of his butt works because it sounds half-true. The specificity of 'strangely' (self-aware about how odd the pride is) elevates it beyond a simple 'I think I'm attractive' joke.

jokes.text: It's kind of a risky joke, Tag. And what is this drawing? I can't figure out what this is. / You're looking at it upside down... You know what? It doesn't matter.
jokes.setup: Mr. Zelner examines the pornographic sketch in the evaluation.
jokes.punchline: Tag begins to helpfully orient the drawing ('You're looking at it upside down') before thinking better of it.
jokes.explanation: Tag's reflexive helpfulness in correctly orienting the pornographic sketch before catching himself is excellent cringe comedy. The abrupt self-correction ('You know what? It doesn't matter') is a perfect button. This is good escalation of the evaluation subplot.

jokes.text: Hell, I even enjoy a naughty limerick every now and then. But there's a time and a place, huh? / Unless you, uh, have a limerick right now. / No? Okay. Well, uh, you've got my fax number.
jokes.setup: Mr. Zelner delivers a stern speech about appropriate workplace humor.
jokes.punchline: He immediately undercuts his own moral authority by asking if Tag has a naughty limerick on hand — and when he doesn't, provides his fax number for future delivery.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and the best use of a guest character. Mr. Zelner's moral authority completely collapses — he goes from reprimanding Tag to soliciting a naughty limerick, then leaving his fax number for one. The structure is excellent: stern lecture, sudden hypocrisy, practical follow-through ('you've got my fax number'). The fax number detail is perfect — specific, dated, and absolutely commits to the bit. Earns its 8+.

jokes.text: Are you kidding me? With a cute butt like this, I'd find work.
jokes.setup: Rachel thanks Tag for taking the blame, noting he could have lost his job.
jokes.punchline: Tag's confidence that his 'cute butt' is a viable career asset is both vain and charming.
jokes.explanation: Good callback button to the tushy thread. Tag's breezy confidence in his butt as a job-finding asset is in character for him as an attractive young man. 'I'd find work' is a good, economical button.

jokes.text: Tag sweeps the desk again, then Rachel says: 'What? / It's just... it took me so long to get that desk organized.' / I'm sorry. / There it is.
jokes.setup: In a romantic moment, Tag sweeps Rachel's desk clean (mirroring what Rachel did earlier).
jokes.punchline: Rachel's response is not romantic — she's annoyed about her carefully organized desk. Tag says 'I'm sorry.' Rachel's 'There it is' is a wry callback to her own earlier desk-sweep.
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback structure. Tag imitates Rachel's earlier romantic move; Rachel's reaction (annoyed about organization rather than swooning) mirrors her own earlier request to 'help clean this up.' 'There it is' as a wry acknowledgment completes the circle beautifully. The joke rewards attentive viewing.

jokes.text: We're waiting for the candy. Bring out the candy. / Yeah, lady, give us candy.
jokes.setup: Monica discovers a crowd of neighbors waiting outside her apartment for candy.
jokes.punchline: The mob has fully formed — neighbors are shouting for candy like an angry crowd demanding tribute.
jokes.explanation: The candy obsession has escalated to mob proportions, which is funny. The image of neighbors chanting for candy like an angry crowd is a solid visual comedy moment.

jokes.text: Hey, and you cannot smoke in here.
jokes.setup: Joey has led the candy crowd into the apartment; Chandler is watching the chaos.
jokes.punchline: Among all the chaos, Chandler specifically calls out the person smoking indoors — implying 'smokes-a-lot lady' has followed everyone inside.
jokes.explanation: Small but satisfying callback to 'smokes-a-lot lady' from the opening scenes — she has indeed followed the crowd inside and is smoking. Good payoff for a minor setup.

jokes.text: Merry Christmas.
jokes.setup: Chandler has dragged Joey inside to confront him about being in the candy mob
jokes.punchline: Joey's response to being caught waiting in line for his friend's girlfriend's candy: a cheerful 'Merry Christmas'
jokes.explanation: Perfect Joey response. Two words, complete economy, entirely character-specific. Joey has zero shame about being in the candy mob and greets Chandler's confrontation with seasonal cheer. The non-sequitur greeting sidesteps any need to explain himself. Very Joey.

jokes.text: Candy Lady? / No, not 'Candy Lady.' / If we know it, can we have candy?
jokes.setup: Chandler shames the neighbors for not knowing Monica's name after eating her candy for days.
jokes.punchline: A neighbor guesses 'Candy Lady' (not a name); Monica denies it; a different neighbor asks if knowing her name earns candy — missing the entire moral lesson.
jokes.explanation: 'Candy Lady' as a sincere answer to 'what is her name' is funny, and the follow-up question ('If we know it, can we have candy?') shows the neighbors have completely absorbed the candy obsession as transactional motivation. Good mob comedy.

jokes.text: Did you smoke? / No, smokes-a-lot lady blew smoke directly into my mouth.
jokes.setup: Chandler returns smelling of smoke after dealing with the candy mob.
jokes.punchline: His denial is technically true but the specific image — smoke blown directly into his mouth — is absurd and passive-aggressive.
jokes.explanation: The specific image of smoke blown 'directly into my mouth' is excellently absurd — it implies a very strange and aggressive action from smokes-a-lot lady. Chandler's straight-faced denial while technically not lying is perfect character comedy.

jokes.text: Did you smoke? / No, smokes-a-lot lady blew smoke directly into my mouth.
jokes.setup: Monica notices Chandler smells of smoke after dealing with the candy mob
jokes.punchline: Chandler defensively explains the passive smoking — smokes-a-lot lady blew smoke 'directly into' his mouth, which is both specific and absurd
jokes.explanation: The 'directly into my mouth' detail is excellent — it's hyper-specific and implies a weird intimate proximity with smokes-a-lot lady. The callback to the established character pays off. Chandler's defensiveness ('No,') followed by this explanation is well-timed.

jokes.text: I'm fine now, but it was really scary there for a while. Someone slipped a threatening note under the door. / Oh, yeah. Sorry about that. Mob mentality or whatever. I don't know.
jokes.setup: Monica describes how terrifying the candy mob became, including a threatening note.
jokes.punchline: The neighbor casually admits to writing the threatening note and excuses it with 'mob mentality or whatever.'
jokes.explanation: 'Mob mentality or whatever. I don't know.' as a breezy explanation for writing a threatening note to your neighbor is a great character moment. The casualness of the excuse is funnier than any elaborate justification would be.

jokes.text: Oh, yeah. Sorry about that. Mob mentality or whatever. I don't know.
jokes.setup: Chandler reveals someone slipped a threatening note under the door during the candy standoff
jokes.punchline: Gary casually confesses he wrote it, then dismisses it with 'mob mentality or whatever' — as if that fully explains and excuses threatening someone over candy
jokes.explanation: Gary's casual admission and even more casual dismissal — 'mob mentality or whatever, I don't know' — is a great punchline. The shrug embedded in 'or whatever' is perfect. Someone who writes threatening notes over candy and immediately apologizes with zero shame is a funny character note.

jokes.text: Don't be so corny, Ross. It's not an After School Special.
jokes.setup: Ross delivers a sincere, saccharine speech about Phoebe overcoming her fears after she successfully rides the bike.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe calls the speech out as 'an After School Special' — a slight meta-awareness that Ross is performing a TV-style moral lesson.
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's self-awareness about narrative cheese is funny and meta without being too winking. 'After School Special' is a specific enough cultural reference to land well. Good button for the bike subplot.

tmdb_overview: When Phoebe tells the gang about how she was too poor to have a bike as a child, Ross goes out and buys her one. While Phoebe absolutely loves the bike, the gang soon discovers that she doesn't actually know how to ride one. Meanwhile, Monica decides to make candy in order to get to know her neighbours, and while they all love the candy, nobody is particularly interested in Monica herself. Rachel and Tag try to hide their relationship at work, but things go awry when Rachel writes a playful work evaluation of Tag that he accidentally turns in to Human Resources.
insight: Chandler's candy obsession drives 14 of 37 jokes in a mid-tier episode.
